newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian banks face tough competition - officials.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian banks face tough competition - officials.

text.p: Increasing penetration by international banks is sharpening competition and changing the face of Hungary's corporate and retail banking sector, the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Wednesday.
"Almost half of the total registered capital of banks is in the hands of foreigners," NBH department head Ferenc Karvalits told journalists at a banking conference.
The conference came just days after Hungary faced its
biggest banking crisis in years when a run on Postabank, the country's second largest bank, resulted in withdrawals of more than 20 billion forints ($113 million) in a little more than four days.
Finance Ministry State Secretery Agnes Balazs said she believed the panic could have happened anywhere in the region.
"The rumours happened to start in Hungary rather than somewhere else," she told Reuters. "Depositors (in other countries of central and Eastern Europe) have not really been tested yet."
"We have to draw conclusions and find out why the population, which saves a lot even by European standards, is so nervous," she added.

Officials who spoke at the conference, which was closed to the press, said they did not see any lasting ill effect for the banking system from the run, which ended on Monday after regulators said Postabank was sound.

Karvalits noted that the structure of Hungary's commercial banking sector, which replaced a communist-type centralised system 10 years ago, had changed fundamentally in the past few years as foreign joint venture banks took a substantial part of the corporate business from large state-owned banks.
"Now there are six to eight main players on the corporate market," he said. "Their size is similar, and they compete on their own terms."
Karvalits added that having earlier concentrated on winning the largest companies as clients, the foreign owners were now turning towards medium-size companies.
"They have accumulated so much capital here that they have to find new business to best utilise the capital," he said.

He added that he also expected large changes in the next three years in the retail banking market, for which competition was sharply increasing under the influence of some international investors which had acquired controlling stakes in state-owned banks.
"There are three or four players which will attack retail services," Karvalics said. "These include General Electric, ABN Amro and ING."
General Electric Capital Services has a stake in Budapest Bank, ABN Amro bought Magyar Hitel Bank (MHB) and ING's Budapest subsidiary has taken over parts of Dunabank.

The three privatised Hungarian banks had strong positions in retail banking, and with the backing of foreign owners they would compete hard with OTP, which is traditionally dominant in Hungary's retail market, Karvalics said.
"(The new owners ) have capital, products, an international reputation and they are big and strong," he said.
But OTP had prepared well for sharper competition, he added.

"OTP is fighting well, particularly in product development and business policies, and is increasing the number of accounts and cards at an amazing pace," he said. "If they can keep up this pace, it could do them a lot of good."
Hungary would continue bank privatisation and this would pose a major challenge to domestic banks, Finance Ministry State Secretary Agnes Balazs told journalists.

"Nobody can expect protection for the domestic banks to be kept up for long," she said. "Hungarian bankers must learn to think in global dimensions and privatisation must have a crucial role in that."
($ = 177.3 Hungarian Forints)
